title: Descartes Colloquium: From Genesis to Normativity in Brouwer's Intuitionism / Ernest Nagel's Peircean Philosophy of Science
speaker: Silviu-Constantin Federovici (Alexandru Ioan Cuza University of Iași) and Mousa Mohammadian (American University of Beirut)
location: Johanna Hudig building, room 1.27 (Alex Brenninkmeijer room), entrance Kromme Nieuwegracht 47E
description: Descartes Centre Colloquium on history & philosophy of science (replaces the UPAC Colloquium this week). Two talks. Hybrid; e-mail dc-colloquium@uu.nl for the Teams link.
abstract:
Silviu-Constantin Federovici, "From Genesis to Normativity in Brouwer's Intuitionism":
Intuitionism is considered a systematic challenge to certain classical principles of mathematics, yet its viability as a substitute remains widely contested (e.g., Tait 1983). While this objection concerns its capacity to supplant classical results, Brouwer's intention to explain "how mathematics is rooted in life" (Brouwer 1906, in van Dalen 2011, p. 27) invites another interpretative approach, namely a more fundamental epistemological inquiry into the relationship between mental experience and the constitution of mathematical constructions. Building on genetic investigations into Brouwer's philosophical works (van Stigt 1990, p. xii; van Atten 2004, pp. 2–3), this talk examines two interconnected dimensions of his intuitionism: the mental background from which mathematics emerges as a distinctive field of knowledge and the norms governing constructions within it. More specifically, the analysis centres on a tripartite genetic model of intuition, volition, and reflexivity, exploring how these faculties furnish evidence for the legitimacy of intuitionistic constructions. Selected mathematical examples and archival materials will help trace this connection. Finally, the talk addresses the issue of psychologism: can the genetic-normative structure be coherently articulated without reducing mathematical reasoning to contingent states of mind, and what remains philosophically valuable even if the full complementarity of these two dimensions cannot be established?

Mousa Mohammadian, "Ernest Nagel's Peircean Philosophy of Science":
This talk traces the Peircean themes that run through Ernest Nagel's philosophy of science from his earliest writings in the 1920s to his mature work around 1960. Although Nagel's relation to logical empiricism has received considerable attention, the continuing importance of C. S. Peirce for his philosophical development has been less fully recognized. I bring this Peircean strand to the foreground by examining Nagel's treatment of inquiry, logic, measurement, probability, scientific method, and the relation between theory and experience. The talk argues that Peirce provides an important and persistent framework for understanding the development and distinctive character of Nagel's philosophy of science.
